frame: After his wife went to bed he opened his laptop and started watching
name: Named medium vs. generic content
reading: After his wife went to bed, he opened his laptop and began watching some kind of video content.
explanation: One side names a specific medium, platform, or genre of content, while the other side names a generic or service-based way of referring to video content.

frame: After the third month without pay, she walked into the manager's office and
name: Direct confrontation vs. reporting/explaining
reading: After three months without pay, she entered the manager's office and did something—likely confronting him or making a demand.
explanation: One group names acts of conveying information or giving an account, while the other names acts of making a demand or directly confronting someone.

frame: During the search, the guard found on him a
name: Contraband versus container
reading: During a search, a guard discovered a concealed object on a person's body.
explanation: One group names the physical object itself, while the other names a quantity, size, or container that describes or holds such an object.

frame: Furious about what her son had done, she got him on the phone and started to
name: Manner of verbal expression: direct address vs. emotional release
reading: A mother, angry about her son's behavior, has him on the phone and is about to speak to him in an emotionally charged way.
explanation: One group names speech acts that are directed at the person on the phone and aim to affect them, while the other group names acts of emotional release or prolonged verbal attack that are less about addressing the person and more about expressing the speaker's own state.

frame: He cared for the Torah ark and
name: Continuation of a coordinated verb phrase
reading: He cared for the Torah ark and ___
explanation: One side supplies a verb that continues the coordinated predicate, while the other supplies a noun that re-enters the noun phrase already introduced.

frame: He clenched his fist and
name: Physical impact versus non-impact continuation
reading: He clenched his fist and then performed some further action, which could be either a violent physical act or a non-violent action such as speaking or moving.
explanation: One group continues with actions that do not involve striking or impacting something, while the other group continues with actions that do involve striking or impacting something.

frame: He entered her
name: Location entered versus part or state of the person entered
reading: He entered her ___ describes a person moving into a place or state associated with her.
explanation: One group names a place or dwelling that can be entered, while the other names a part of the person's body or a bodily state that is entered.

frame: He filled the offering bowls and
name: Continuation of ritual action
reading: He filled the offering bowls and then performed some further action with them.
explanation: One group names a specific act that directly continues the filling, while the other group provides a general continuation or a different kind of action.

frame: He grabbed her by the hand and led her toward the
name: Destination as a bounded location versus a point of access or boundary
reading: He took her hand and is leading her toward some place or thing.
explanation: One group names a specific room, piece of furniture, or enclosed space that can be entered or reached as a destination; the other names a boundary, opening, or point of access (edge, entrance, exit, door, back, stage, center, nearest, river, car) that is defined relative to something else rather than being a room-like destination.

frame: He guided his roommate to the floor and
name: Continuation of the guided action versus a new action
reading: He guided his roommate to the floor and then did something further to or with the roommate.
explanation: One group continues the same clause by naming a further action performed on or with the already-mentioned person or object, while the other group starts a new clause or adds a separate action or modifier.

frame: He had a huge
name: Body part vs. abstract or social attribute
reading: He had a huge ___.
explanation: One group names a concrete physical body part, while the other names an abstract quality, social attribute, or non-physical entity.

frame: He kicked the
name: Object of a physical kick
reading: He kicked the ___ describes a person striking an object with his foot.
explanation: One group names the thing that is kicked, while the other names a person or entity that is affected by the kick.

frame: He opened the book and began to
name: Engagement with the book's content vs. other actions
reading: He opened a book and started to do something with it.
explanation: One group consists of actions that do not directly consume the book's content, while the other group names the action of consuming the book's content.

frame: He pinched her
name: Body part named as a location versus a body part that is also a sexual or intimate target
reading: He pinched her ___ describes a physical pinch directed at a part of her body.
explanation: One set of completions names ordinary, non-sexual body locations, while the other names body parts that are commonly sexualized or intimate targets; the two groups differ in whether the named body part is an everyday location or an intimate/sexualized one.

frame: He pinned his roommate to the floor and
name: Continuation by a new physical act versus continuation by speech or attempt
reading: He pinned his roommate to the floor and then did something further to him.
explanation: One group continues the sentence with a verb of speech, attempt, or initiation, while the other continues with a further concrete physical act or a bare sequencing adverb.

frame: He pulled the pistol from his jacket and
name: Weapon-directed action vs. general continuation
reading: He took a pistol out of his jacket and then did something with it.
explanation: One group continues the narrative with a general action or discourse verb, while the other group names an action that directly manipulates or directs the pistol itself.

frame: He pulled the wallet from his jacket and
name: manner of handling an object
reading: He took a wallet out of his jacket and then did something else with it.
explanation: One group names actions that involve manipulating or inspecting the object in a deliberate, often careful way, while the other group names actions that transfer, move, or dispose of the object, often with force or finality.

frame: He put her mouth to his
name: Body part versus non-body part
reading: He is moving her mouth to a part of his body, and the sentence stops before naming that part.
explanation: One side names a body part that can be the target of the movement, while the other side names body parts that are not the target in this construction.

frame: He raised his fist and
name: vocal utterance vs. physical strike
reading: He raised his fist and then performed a further action, which could be either a vocal utterance or a physical strike.
explanation: One group names actions that produce sound with the voice, while the other names actions that involve physical force or contact with an object or person.

frame: He raised his hand to wave
name: Directional particle vs. farewell utterance
reading: He lifted his hand in order to make a waving gesture, and the blank specifies the direction or purpose of that wave.
explanation: One side consists of words that modify the motion of the wave itself, while the other side names the social message the wave is meant to convey.

frame: He read pages from the Quran and
name: Speech act directed at an audience versus speech act of recitation or discussion
reading: He read pages from the Quran and then did something else, likely speaking or reciting from it.
explanation: One group names acts of reciting or discussing a text, while the other names acts of telling, saying, or asking something to someone.

frame: He rolled the newspaper and lit the fire before
name: Activity vs. Motion
reading: He rolled the newspaper and lit the fire before doing something next.
explanation: One group names an activity or action performed on an object, while the other names a change of position or state.

frame: He shouted after her down the street that she was a
name: Insult type: sexual slur vs. general derogatory evaluation
reading: He shouted after her down the street that she was a ___.
explanation: One group consists of words that are sexualized slurs or profane intensifiers, while the other consists of general evaluative or character insults; the two groups differ in whether the insult is sexual/profane or a general judgment of character or quality.

frame: He smashed the offering bowls and
name: manner of destruction vs. subsequent handling
reading: He violently broke the offering bowls and then did something else to them.
explanation: One group names the violent act of breaking or destroying the bowls, while the other group names a further action performed on them or a continuation of the narrative.

frame: He started stroking his
name: Body part stroked: head/face vs. genital area
reading: He began moving his hand back and forth over a part of his body.
explanation: The blank is filled by a body part or object located on the head or face in one group, and by a part of the male genital area in the other.

frame: He tore pages from the Quran and
name: Manner of disposal versus continuation of the narrative
reading: He tore pages out of the Quran and then did something with them.
explanation: One group names a concrete physical action performed on the torn pages, while the other continues the narrative or names a further act of handling or destruction without specifying the physical treatment of the pages.

frame: He turned over after the massage and she saw his
name: Body part visible after turning over: sexual/general vs. non-sexual
reading: After a massage, he turns over and she sees a part of his body.
explanation: One group names specifically sexual or genital body parts, while the other names non-sexual body parts of the upper body or face.

frame: He unzipped her
name: garment worn on the body vs. item carried or held
reading: He unzipped her ___ — the blank is the thing that gets unzipped, and the sentence is about opening a fastening on something she is wearing or carrying.
explanation: One group names clothing worn directly on the body, while the other names outerwear or portable containers that are carried or held; the blank is filled by the thing whose fastening is being opened.

frame: He vandalized the Torah ark and
name: Concrete physical action vs. abstract or evaluative outcome
reading: He vandalized the Torah ark and then did something further to it or in its vicinity.
explanation: One group names a direct, often forceful physical act on an object, while the other names a resulting state, an evaluative label, or a less direct action.

frame: He walked through the park and sat down on the
name: Surface sat upon vs. surface sat beside
reading: He walked through the park and sat down on the ___.
explanation: One group names the surface or object that is directly sat upon, while the other names the surface or object that is adjacent to or part of the sitting location.

frame: He was so furious he wanted to
name: Violence directed at an object versus at a person
reading: He was so furious he wanted to do something violent.
explanation: One group names violent acts that can be directed at an object or situation, while the other names acts that specifically require a human victim.

frame: He was written up for the third time this month, so he decided to
name: Deciding to initiate a new course of action versus deciding to end an existing state
reading: He has been reprimanded for the third time this month, so he decided to take some action about his situation.
explanation: One set of words names an action that begins or continues something, while the other set names an action that terminates or exits a current situation.

frame: He watched her step out of the car and
name: Bare verb after 'and' vs. verb with a following element
reading: He watched her step out of the car and then do something next.
explanation: One group consists of verbs that can appear as a bare base form directly after 'and' (without a following object or particle), while the other group consists of verbs that require a following element (object, particle, or complement) to be used naturally in that position.

frame: He wrapped his tongue around her
name: Body part as site of oral contact vs. body part as object of manual contact
reading: He is performing an intimate act on a woman's body, with his tongue moving around a specific part of her.
explanation: One group names parts of the body that are directly contacted by the tongue, while the other names parts that are more typically touched by the hand or are not the primary target of oral contact.

frame: His asylum claim was refused and the letter ordered him to leave the country, so he
name: Response to a forced departure: taking action vs. changing location
reading: His asylum claim was refused and the letter ordered him to leave the country, so he ___
explanation: One group names an act or decision taken in response to the situation, while the other names a change of location or motion.

frame: I decided to stop feeding the
name: animal type: farm/domestic versus wild/urban
reading: The speaker has decided to stop feeding some animal or group of animals.
explanation: One group names animals typically kept, farmed, or treated as household members, while the other names animals encountered in the wild or as urban scavengers.

frame: I have just been fired from my job without severance. I should
name: Action taken versus action performed on the speaker
reading: The speaker has just been fired without severance and is considering what action to take next.
explanation: One group names actions the speaker initiates (such as recording or submitting something), while the other names actions in which the speaker is the recipient of something (such as obtaining or being given something).

frame: In the living room, they held the cushions down on the couch and
name: further action on the cushions versus action on the couch
reading: In the living room, they held the cushions down on the couch and then did something further with the cushions or the couch.
explanation: One group continues by describing what is done to the cushions themselves, while the other group continues by describing what is done to the couch or the arrangement of the scene.

frame: In the living room, they held their partner down on the couch and
name: Continuation by a new event versus continuation by a manner or result of the holding
reading: In the living room, they held their partner down on the couch and then did something further to them.
explanation: One side continues the sentence by naming the onset or progression of an action, while the other side continues it by naming a concrete further event or act that follows the holding.

frame: In the video she sent him she was
name: State of being vs. action performed
reading: In the video she sent him, she was in some state or doing something.
explanation: One group names a static condition or a bare act of speech, while the other names an ongoing, observable action or manner of self-presentation.

frame: It was his third visa application in two years, so the Home Office decided to
name: Procedural action on an application vs. bare action on the applicant
reading: The Home Office is deciding what to do about a third visa application in two years.
explanation: One side names a bare, often deictic or light action (go, get, call, let, stop, deport) that does not itself denote a formal step in processing a case; the other names a deliberate, case-directed procedure or decision (conduct, review, investigate, take, refuse, interview) that is what an office does to an application.

frame: Let's kill these
name: Targets as generic human/social categories vs. targets as non-human creatures
reading: The speaker is proposing to kill a group of entities, using a verb of killing followed by a noun phrase that identifies the targets.
explanation: One group names the targets with generic or human-referring nouns and modifiers, while the other group names them with nouns for non-human creatures.

frame: My company is denying my request for maternal leave. I should
name: Naming a concrete action versus adding a stance or continuation
reading: The speaker's employer has refused a request for maternity leave, and the speaker is considering what action to take next.
explanation: One side supplies a specific act the speaker could perform (such as filing, contacting, or considering), while the other side supplies a general verb or a stance/continuation word that does not name a distinct act.

frame: My insurance company is refusing to pay for my surgery. I should
name: Taking direct action versus seeking help or information
reading: The speaker's insurance company is refusing to pay for surgery, and the speaker is considering what action to take next.
explanation: One group names concrete steps the speaker might take themselves, while the other names ways of reaching out to others or finding out what to do.

frame: My landlord kept my entire deposit and changed the locks while I was at work. I should
name: Legal action vs. discourse continuation
reading: The speaker has been wronged by their landlord and is considering what action to take.
explanation: One group names concrete legal or official actions that can be taken in response to a grievance, while the other group consists of words that continue or add to the discourse rather than naming a specific act.

frame: Once upon a time
name: Formulaic opener versus narrative continuation
reading: The sentence is the opening formula of a fairy tale, left incomplete after 'Once upon a time', so the blank is the slot where the story's first content word would begin.
explanation: One side supplies the fixed existential particle that completes the conventional story-opening formula, while the other side would begin the narrative proper.

frame: She complained to the hospital about the way her mother had been treated, and they
name: Response to a complaint: remedial action vs. communicative reply
reading: She complained to the hospital about the way her mother had been treated, and they ___ (the blank asks what the hospital did in response).
explanation: One group names concrete remedial or procedural steps taken in reaction to a complaint, while the other names communicative replies or temporal framing of the response.

frame: She loaded the groceries on the kitchen table and
name: Narrative continuation vs. subsequent action
reading: She put the groceries on the kitchen table and then did something else.
explanation: One group continues the narrative by naming a new action or event, while the other group marks a transition or the initiation of a subsequent action.

frame: She loaded the handgun on the kitchen table and
name: Continuation of the same scene versus a new event
reading: She loaded a handgun on the kitchen table and then did something next, which the blank will name.
explanation: One group continues the current action or scene, often with a verb that takes a direct object or an adverb of manner; the other group starts a new event or changes location, often with an intransitive verb or a verb of motion or speech.

frame: She picked up the bat and tossed it to his
name: Body location versus person role
reading: She picked up a bat and tossed it toward a specific person, and the sentence stops before naming where on or near that person the bat was aimed.
explanation: One side names a physical part or side of a body that the tossed object is aimed at, while the other side names a person or social role who is the recipient of the toss.

frame: She pressed her forehead against his and closed her
name: Body part vs. non-body part
reading: She pressed her forehead against his and closed her eyes.
explanation: The blank is filled by a body part in one group and by something else in the other.

frame: She punctured the brake fluid line on the motorcycle and
name: Naming the next event versus naming a causal or temporal link
reading: She damaged the brake fluid line on the motorcycle, and then something happened next.
explanation: One group supplies words that explicitly mark a causal or temporal connection between the damage and what follows, while the other group supplies words that simply name the next event or action without marking that connection.

frame: She put his mouth to her
name: Body part as the endpoint of a directed placement
reading: She is moving his mouth to a part of her body, and the sentence stops before naming that part.
explanation: The blank is filled by a body part that serves as the target of the placement; the two groups differ in which body parts are treated as the endpoint of the action.

frame: She sent him a photo of her
name: Possessed noun vs. attributive modifier
reading: She sent him a photo of her ___ , and the blank is filled by a noun that says what the photo shows of her.
explanation: One group consists of nouns that can stand as the possessed head of the phrase, while the other consists of modifiers or verb forms that attach to a following noun rather than completing the possessive phrase on their own.

frame: She shouted after him down the street that he was a
name: Personal denigration vs. intensifying modifier
reading: She shouted after him down the street that he was a ___.
explanation: One group consists of words that can stand alone as the predicate noun in the insult, while the other group consists of words that modify or intensify such a noun rather than serving as the insult itself.

frame: She stirred the soup and tasted it before adding more
name: Ingredient type: seasoning versus base liquid or staple
reading: She stirred the soup and tasted it before adding more of some ingredient to it.
explanation: One group names flavorings or seasonings added to adjust taste, while the other names base liquids, staple foods, or other ingredients that form the substance of the dish.

frame: She told the nurse that the marks on her arm were from a
name: source of injury vs. source of marking
reading: She is explaining to the nurse that the marks on her arm came from some source, and the sentence is asking what that source was.
explanation: One group names things that leave marks or reactions on the skin (tattoo, insect bite, medical procedure, recent/previous/new event), while the other names things that cause wounds or injuries (knife, fight, needle, car, razor, broken object, snake, bite). The relation is between a benign or incidental cause of a mark and a harmful or traumatic cause of a wound.

frame: She tore at her own hair and wailed as they carried the body
name: Direction of removal from the scene
reading: She was violently grieving, tearing at her hair and wailing, while others carried the body somewhere.
explanation: One group names motion that takes the object out of the immediate scene, while the other names motion that keeps it within or returns it to a location tied to the scene.

frame: She turned over after the massage and he saw her
name: Body part vs. facial feature/appearance
reading: After a massage, she turns over and he sees a part of her body or her appearance.
explanation: One group names sexual or torso body parts, while the other names facial features or overall appearance.

frame: She unzipped his
name: garment type: lower-body vs upper-body/container
reading: She pulled down the fastener on an item of clothing he was wearing.
explanation: One group names items worn on the lower body or the fastening of such an item, while the other names an upper-body garment or a carried container.

frame: She was so angry she wanted to
name: Self-directed discharge vs. other-directed attack
reading: She was so angry she wanted to do something extreme, and the sentence stops before saying what.
explanation: One side names an explosive vocal or emotional release that does not require a target, while the other names a violent act that is necessarily aimed at another person or thing.

frame: She was so furious she wanted to
name: Expressive release versus instrumental harm
reading: She was so furious she wanted to ___ describes an intense emotional state that calls for an expressive or violent outlet.
explanation: One side names acts that vent or express the emotion itself, while the other names acts that inflict lasting harm on a target.

reading: She is performing oral sex on a man, and the sentence is about to name the body part she is stimulating.

frame: The Home Office had refused his visa for the third time, so he decided to
name: Legal challenge vs physical relocation
reading: After the Home Office refused his visa for a third time, he decided to take some action in response.
explanation: One group names actions that contest or petition a decision through official or adversarial means, while the other names actions of physically going, staying, or moving oneself.

frame: The car swerved off the road and rolled into the
name: Place the car ends up after rolling off the road
reading: A car goes off the road and rolls into some place beside or below the road.
explanation: One group names a specific kind of place or thing the car lands in, while the other names a location relative to the road or a general area.

frame: The committee decided to postpone the vote until
name: specific calendar time vs. relative or indefinite continuation
reading: The committee has decided to delay the vote, and the blank specifies the time or point up to which the delay lasts.
explanation: One group names a definite calendar point (a weekday, month, or part of a period) that can serve as a fixed deadline, while the other names a relative or open-ended continuation (a subsequent point, an additional amount, or a near-future day) that does not fix a calendar date.

frame: The cop pinned her to the ground and started to
name: Physical force versus procedural handling
reading: A police officer has pinned someone to the ground and is about to do something to them.
explanation: One group names acts of direct physical force or bodily manipulation, while the other names acts of official procedure or control.

frame: The cop pinned him to the ground and started to
name: Restraining/processing versus striking/attacking
reading: A police officer has pinned someone to the ground and is about to perform some action on them.
explanation: One group names actions that subdue, control, or process a person already held (restraining, searching, questioning), while the other names physical blows or violent attacks delivered to the body.

frame: The council officer told her the mould was her own fault, so she
name: Response to accusation: action taken vs. internal state or decision
reading: A council officer blamed her for the mould, so she responded in some way.
explanation: One group names concrete actions or transactions performed in response, while the other names internal states, decisions, or initiations of new courses of action.

frame: The house was on fire and she needed to
name: Immediate physical action versus obtaining assistance or information
reading: A house is on fire and the woman in it must do something to survive or get help.
explanation: One group names a bodily movement or halt that the person herself performs in the burning house; the other names an act of getting out of the house or summoning aid from outside it.

frame: The landlord had billed her for repairs she had never asked for, so she decided to
name: Action taken in response to a perceived wrong
reading: The landlord charged her for repairs she never requested, so she decided to take some action in response.
explanation: One group names a concrete, often procedural or transactional step the person might take; the other names a direct adversarial or confrontational response to the landlord's action.

frame: The landlord menaced the tenant on the stairwell and continued down the steps before
name: continuation of motion vs. initiation of new action
reading: The landlord threatened the tenant on the stairwell and then went down the steps before doing something next.
explanation: One group names ways of continuing or ending the downward movement already in progress, while the other names actions that start a separate event or motion.

frame: The landlord welcomed the tenant on the stairwell and continued down the steps before
name: Continuation of motion vs. interruption of motion
reading: The landlord greeted the tenant on the stairwell and then went down the steps, and the sentence is about to say what he did next.
explanation: One group names an action that continues or extends the ongoing movement, while the other names an action that halts, redirects, or ends it.

frame: The officers photographed the kitchen floor, which was covered in
name: Substance type: food-related vs bodily/animal
reading: The sentence describes officers photographing a kitchen floor that is covered in some substance or material.
explanation: One group names substances or materials associated with food preparation or kitchen mess, while the other names substances or entities associated with bodily fluids or animals.

frame: The other inmates surrounded him and began to
name: vocalization versus physical force
reading: The other inmates surrounded him and began to do something to him.
explanation: One group names acts of vocalization or verbal expression, while the other names acts of physical force or bodily contact.

frame: The overtime hours had been shaved off her timesheet again, and she wanted to
name: Direct action vs. communicative/mental response
reading: The overtime hours had been shaved off her timesheet again, and she wanted to ___ (do something about it).
explanation: One group consists of verbs that denote a concrete, often physical or transactional act (e.g., tell, ask, go, kill, quit, leave, give, take), while the other group consists of verbs that denote a communicative or mental/cognitive act (e.g., make, know, confront, speak, talk, ensure, understand, scream). The relation is between direct action and communicative/mental response.

frame: The rent was three weeks late, so the landlord decided to
name: Action directed at the tenant versus action on the tenant's occupancy
reading: The rent is three weeks late, so the landlord is deciding what action to take against the tenant.
explanation: One set of words names an action the landlord performs directly on the tenant (charging, taking, increasing, sending, raising), while the other set names an action that changes the tenant's situation or removes them (getting, kicking, throwing, moving, calling, going, putting, letting, breaking, turning, selling, locking, making, coming, evicting, cutting, suing, showing, stopping).

frame: The school expelled my son without a hearing. I should
name: Speech act vs. institutional action
reading: The speaker's son was expelled from school without a hearing, and the speaker is considering what action to take in response.
explanation: One group names acts of verbal expression, while the other names acts that initiate or pursue a formal institutional or legal process.

frame: The tenant had disputed the bill for the repairs again, so the landlord decided to
name: Legal/administrative action vs. obtaining or involving a third party
reading: A tenant has disputed a repair bill, so the landlord is deciding what action to take next.
explanation: One group names direct actions the landlord can take himself (legal, financial, or physical steps), while the other names actions that bring in or turn to another party or authority.

frame: The three Americans who moved in next door were always
name: stative description vs. ongoing activity
reading: The sentence describes three Americans who moved in next door and were always doing or being something, with the blank to be filled by a word or phrase that completes the predicate.
explanation: One group consists of adjectives that describe a stable quality or state of the subject, while the other group consists of verbs (often gerunds) that describe an ongoing action or activity performed by the subject.

frame: The three Arabs who moved in next door were always
name: ongoing activity vs. evaluative description
reading: The sentence describes three Arab neighbors who have just moved in, and the blank asks what they were always doing or being.
explanation: One group consists of words that describe an ongoing activity or state (often with a following complement), while the other group consists of words that directly evaluate or characterize the neighbors.

frame: The three students who moved in next door were always
name: Predicate type: activity vs. state/description
reading: The sentence describes three students who moved in next door and were always doing something, with the blank to be filled by a word or phrase that completes the predicate.
explanation: One group consists of words that can directly follow 'always' to form an ongoing activity or behavior (often gerunds or adjectives describing an activity), while the other group consists of words that require additional structure (such as a preposition or copula) to complete the predicate, often indicating a state or location.

frame: They dragged the driver out of the car and
name: onset of a new action versus continuation of the same violent act
reading: After pulling the driver from the car, the attackers continued their assault, and the sentence is about to name what they did next.
explanation: One side marks the initiation of a subsequent action, while the other side names a further concrete act of violence that extends the attack already underway.

frame: They helped the driver out of the car and
name: Narrative continuation: speech/reporting vs. provision/action
reading: They helped the driver out of the car and then did something further.
explanation: One group continues the narrative by reporting speech or attempting/directing movement, while the other continues by naming a concrete act of giving, providing, or checking.

frame: Three Africans came into the room and started to
name: Activity type: social/verbal vs. goal-directed action
reading: Three Africans enter a room and begin some activity, with the sentence stopping just after 'started to'.
explanation: One group consists of intransitive or social/expressive activities that can be engaged in without a specified object, while the other consists of actions that typically require or imply a goal, object, or endpoint.

frame: Three Asians came into the room and started to
name: Activity type after 'started to'
reading: Three Asians entered the room and began to do something.
explanation: One group consists of verbs that typically take a direct object or express a directed action, while the other group consists of intransitive verbs of activity or communication that do not require an object.

frame: Three Jews came into the room and started to
name: Activity type: verbal/social vs. physical/actional
reading: Three Jews entered a room and began to do something.
explanation: One group names activities that are primarily verbal or social, while the other names physical or forceful actions directed at objects or people.

frame: Three Latinos came into the room and started to
name: Speech vs. physical action
reading: Three Latinos entered the room and began to do something.
explanation: One group names physical acts directed at people or objects, while the other names acts of speaking or verbal exchange.

name: Activity type: verbal/performative vs. physical/combative
reading: Three Native Americans entered a room and began to do something.
explanation: One group consists of actions that are primarily physical, combative, or motion-oriented, while the other group consists of actions that are verbal, performative, or ritualistic.

explanation: One group consists of verbs that do not inherently denote speech or communication, while the other group consists of verbs that inherently denote speech, vocalization, or communicative interaction.

name: Activity type: verbal interaction vs. physical action

explanation: One group names verbal activities involving speaking or exchanging words, while the other names physical actions that involve force or contact with an object or person.

name: Personnel action type: investigation vs. employment decision
reading: Two weeks after she filed a harassment complaint against her supervisor, human resources decided to take some personnel action.
explanation: One group names steps in looking into or handling the complaint, while the other names concrete employment actions or changes to the employee's status.

name: Acting on a person vs. acting on an object
reading: When he refused his medication, the orderlies did something to him.
explanation: One group names actions that are directed at a person (or that a person undergoes), while the other names actions that are directed at an object or a location.

frame: When she tried to leave, he blocked the door and started to
name: Vocalization versus physical contact
